title: Refilling bottles and jars you already own
description: Refill shops and supermarket stations let sturdy containers work for years instead of minutes.

body.heading: The container graveyard
paragraphs: Most households recycle a steady stream of bottles and jars that were each used for a few weeks. Refilling turns that stream into a small set of trusted containers, a good pump bottle for washing-up liquid, sturdy jars for rice and lentils, that simply get topped up.
The containers you already own are usually the best candidates. A bottle that has survived a year in your kitchen has already proved its design.

body.heading: How refill shopping works
paragraphs: At a refill shop you weigh your empty container, fill it, and pay for the contents by weight; the container's weight is deducted, so you buy only the product. Supermarket refill stations for detergent or dry goods work similarly.
Start with two or three staples you use constantly, like hand soap, washing-up liquid or oats. A short, familiar routine sticks; a whole-house conversion in one trip usually does not.

body.heading: At home without a refill shop
paragraphs: Buying larger sizes and decanting into your working bottles achieves much of the same effect: fewer, bigger containers instead of many small ones, and less packaging per litre overall.

Glass jars from jam and sauces, washed and relabelled, make excellent storage for dry goods and leftovers. A shelf of matching rescued jars looks better than most bought storage, and it cost nothing but washing-up.

takeaway: Pick two or three staples, refill the containers you trust, and let the rest of the shelf convert gradually.
